section_6_title: Still have questions? We have answers...
section_6_p_1: A certified translation is a legally recognized translation of a document made by a sworn, certified or authorized translator. This translation is sealed and signed by the translator and certifies its accuracy and completeness compared to the original.
section_6_text_2: What is the difference between apostille and legalization?
section_6_p_2: •Apostille: A simplified procedure for countries that have adhered to the Hague Apostille Convention. The apostille confirms the authenticity of the document and is sufficient for its recognition. • Legalization: Required for countries that are not part of the Apostille Convention. In this case, authentication is carried out in several stages, often up to authentication by the respective embassy.
section_6_p_2_2: •Legalization: Required for countries outside the Apostille Convention. In this case, authentication is carried out in several stages, often up to authentication by the respective embassy.
section_6_text_3: How will my name be displayed in the translation (Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, etc.)?
section_6_p_3: The spelling of the name in the target language must be the same as that on the identity document or identity card to ensure consistency. In some cases, the name is additionally transcribed according to ISO 9, in particular if required by the authority or institution.
section_6_text_4: Should I provide the translator with the original document?
section_6_p_4: In most cases, it is sufficient to provide the translator with a legible or scanned copy of the document. However, depending on the requirements of the authority and specific needs, it may be necessary to provide the translator with the original document. This is particularly the case if the authority requires that the translation be based on the original to ensure authenticity and integrity. It is therefore advisable to clarify this in advance with the translator and the competent authority.
section_6_p_4_2: Note: Authorities often want to see the original document to verify its authenticity. Therefore, make sure you have the original with you when dealing with authorities.
section_6_text_5: What is an apostille and when is it needed?
section_6_p_5: Superauthentication or apostille is an additional certification confirming the authenticity of a document for international legal transactions. It is required in two cases:
section_6_p_5_2: •For the original document: Depending on the country of use, an apostille or legalization is required. This will be done in accordance with German regulations, such as those issued by the regional court (for documents) or the regional council.
section_6_p_5_3: •For certified translation: If the translation is also used abroad, a supercertification of the translator's certification may be required. This is usually requested from the regional court.
section_6_text_6: What to do if the authority has special requirements?
section_6_p_6: Read the letter from the authority carefully. It often contains information about:
section_6_p_6_4: •Responsible bodies where enquiries can be made.
section_6_p_6_5: If you have any questions, please contact the authority directly to avoid misunderstandings.
section_6_text_7: Who can perform a certified translation?
section_6_p_7: In Germany, only sworn, certified or authorised translators, also called court-appointed or court-approved translators, are authorised to issue certified translations. These translators are registered with the courts or with translators' associations.
section_6_text_8: How long does the translation, apostille and legalization process take?
section_6_p_8: • Translation: The normal processing time without express charge is approximately 2 to 5 business days, depending on the size and difficulty of the document. For very large or complex documents, the processing time may be longer. In such cases, we will inform you as soon as possible.
section_6_p_8_2: • Apostille/Legalization: Certification of the certified translation in the form of an apostille or legalization may take approximately 1 to 4 weeks, including postage, depending on the respective regional court or higher regional court. ￼
section_6_p_8_3: Please allow sufficient time, especially if multiple authentication steps are required.
